name: Carlos Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and a junior developer on flood-alert software at a tech company, after checking drains for a contractor and earning a two-year college diploma. I use AI every day to draft tests, though my lead still checks my code and I compare alerts with recorded river levels. Lou, my partner, moves patients and equipment at a hospital; our children are grown, and typical developer pay has helped us save three months of expenses while renting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the flood-alert team that little AI gains are handy for finding a missing comma, but a sensor alert still needs a real reading behind it. I use AI every day to draft test cases, then compare them with last winter’s river log.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 58, a junior after a two-year college diploma, and still have to ask why our alert service rejects a reading. My partner Lou moves patients and equipment in a hospital; with our grown children elsewhere, typical developer pay and three months saved cover our rent, though not every surprise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking the flood alerts against the river log every morning. We would save 110 monthly while both wages continue and keep our old car another year instead of replacing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be calm about the job in this picture, with a little worry about the car. A false flood alarm wakes a street; I want the reading on paper before the message goes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you do before this job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I checked drains for a local contractor, then studied for a two-year diploma when my knees tired of climbing into pits. I know what a blocked grate looks like, but my code skills are still catching up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why use AI every day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me a first test case faster than a blank page. I still run the test against a recorded water level before anyone sees an alert.

I use **AI daily** for draft tests, then verify them.
think: I have **three months saved** and a typical developer wage.
I feel **rent covered**, though our old car may need work.
do: **Check flood alerts** against river logs each morning.
**Save 110 monthly** while both wages continue; keep old car another year.
feel: **Calm** about work, mildly worried about the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI taking planning, checking and coding may write most of the flood-alert tests juniors make. We still need to know who signs off an alert that closes a road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own paid hours could shrink because test writing is much of my day. Three months saved and Lou’s hospital wage give us a route through a short search, but I do not want our rent to rest on one pay slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my lead for approved paid time to learn the new AI sensor-anomaly tool, using historic readings rather than live alerts. If approved, I’d test a false high-water reading weekly; if my hours fall, I’d search paid local drainage software vacancies only where the wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my hours and curious about the new tool. The river will not pause while we argue over a model’s confidence score.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is a false high reading?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A branch can strike the sensor and make the number jump for one minute. I would check the nearby gauge and the time series before a road-closure message.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Lou add hospital shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if shifts are offered and Lou wants them. I would not turn my partner’s extra work into the first line of my plan.

I want **historic readings** used before live AI alerts change.
think: I could lose **paid test-writing hours** as AI improves.
I cannot make **Lou’s possible overtime** part of our rent budget.
do: **Learn anomaly tool** weekly only with lead-approved paid time and historic readings.
**Search paid drainage software** if hours fall and local vacancies cover rent and bills.
feel: **Anxious and curious** about own hours and the new tool.
S1.quote: The river will not pause while we argue over a model’s confidence score.
fieldNote: He seeks **new AI-tool learning** beyond his existing daily test drafting.
Any **job search** follows reduced hours and requires a real bill-covering local vacancy, rather than assuming hospital overtime.

steps.text: Practise AI sensor-anomaly tests weekly only with approved paid time and historic readings
Search paid local drainage-software vacancies if hours fall and wages cover rent and bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write flood-alert code and compare sensor readings cheaper than our team. Robots clearing drains and moving hospital equipment may come around 2031, after my screen work changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the junior job might go quickly, and three months of savings is not enough for a long search. Lou’s porter wage helps, but I would not ask our grown children to replace my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d cancel the plan to replace the car and ask for written notice of any developer cuts. If my job ends after 2028, I’d apply for paid local drain-inspection openings only if vacancies exist, my knees can manage the duties, and wages cover rent and bills; I would ask the public employment office which temporary support we qualify for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed about losing my wage before I know whether a field crew is hiring. A river reading is not a job offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your old contractor take you back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether a paid vacancy exists and whether my knees could handle its duties. I cannot assume the same crew still needs me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a new car for field work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not before a written paid offer and a clear travel requirement. We need the cash for rent first.

say: I expect **AGI in 2028** to reach flood-alert code first.
I expect **drain robots around 2031** to follow later.
think: I may lose **junior developer pay** before finding field work.
I cannot rely on **three months saved** for a long search.
do: **Cancel car replacement** and request written cut notice now.
**Apply for drain inspection** after 2028 job loss only if vacancies fit my knees and wages cover rent and bills.
**Ask public employment office** about actual eligibility if displaced.
feel: **Alarmed** about wage loss before a field vacancy appears.
S2.quote: A river reading is not a job offer.
fieldNote: His **old field work** is a conditional option limited by vacancies and physical ability.
He preserves **rent cash** rather than buying a car before a written paid field offer.

steps.text: Cancel planned car replacement when developer cuts threaten
Apply after 2028 loss only to knee-safe paid drain vacancies covering rent and bills
Ask public employment office about eligibility if displaced

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2031 gives us several years to learn which flood instruments still need someone at the river. Robots clearing drains may follow around 2034, while alert code changes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could return to some field work if I learned the current sensor equipment, though my knees rule out heavy drain clearing. I would need a paid training place, not a course fee taken from our three-month reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the sensor contractor about a paid trainee vacancy and the safety certificate it requires. If a paid place covers rent and bills and the site work fits my knees, I’d enrol and practise one test gauge under a qualified technician, stopping if my knees cannot handle it; we would save 100 monthly while both wages hold, and after 2031 job loss I’d apply only to paid local sensor roles I qualify for and whose wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my code job but able to test a real route with five years. The gauge has to work in rain, not just in a classroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your knee cannot handle the site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stop the field trial and keep looking for paid work I can do safely. I would not accept a job I cannot finish because the title sounds secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who pays for the certificate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The contractor must fund it as part of paid training. I will not spend the rent reserve on a certificate for a job that may not exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2036 gives a decade to test the alert system and build a route into field sensors. Robots clearing drains and moving hospital equipment may arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may still need work at 68 and have not verified a retirement amount, so I will not use one in the budget. If both wages hold, we might build six months of expenses, though the junior role could still end later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep comparing alerts with real river readings and save 120 monthly while both wages continue. I’d take a paid supervised sensor training place if one opens and its wage covers rent and bills; if my developer job ends after 2036, I’d seek a paid qualified local sensor vacancy only if the work fits my knees and wages cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy about changing jobs later, but our current bills look secure for the next few years. A decade gives me time to find out whether my knees and the instruments get along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave coding for an unpaid field trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would keep the developer wage while it exists. I would take only funded paid training that covers bills and that I can do safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move to a river district?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would look at the local contractors and software employers first. Lou’s hospital shifts and our rented home are here, so I am not planning a move.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the junior software wage could end before a paid, knee-safe field opening exists. Written notice, a real drain-inspection vacancy and verified temporary support would help us keep rent paid.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a sensor job would be easier on my knees than drain clearing. I need a supervised paid sensor trial on the actual site before I know whether my knees can handle the work.

headlineQuote: I need a supervised paid sensor trial on the actual site before I know whether my knees can handle the work.
portrait: Carlos is a **58-year-old junior developer** with a two-year diploma, typical pay and three months saved.
He and Lou **rent**; their grown children live independently.
He **uses AI daily** for draft tests and verifies alerts against river readings.
He considers **paid sensor training** only with qualified supervision and work his knees can manage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his junior wage before knee-safe paid field work appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written cut notice**, a real paid field vacancy and verified temporary support would help.
